You cannot declare a target state satisfied; the graph either satisfies it or does not.\\n\\nInvariants:\\n\\n- Gate results and acceptance records pin the predicate version they were evaluated under.\\n- Predicate version bumps invalidate standing evaluated under the old version, exactly like contract bumps.\\n- Names are past participles (N1): `accepted`, `verified`, `integrated`.\\n- A compilation request names a subject and a target predicate; the Driver plans toward the unmet conjuncts.\\n\\nCanonical home: [RFC 0005, Target states](../../rfcs/0005-artifact-lifecycle-and-state-machine/design.md). Catalog: [`catalog/target-states/`](../../catalog/target-states/); shape: [`schema/target-state.schema.json`](../../schema/target-state.schema.json).\\n\",\n    \"docs/concepts/work-graph-build-flow.md\": \"# Work Graph Build Flow {#el:work-graph-build-flow}\\n\\n## Overview {#el:overview}\\n\\nThis page follows one flow end to end: an approved plan goes in, and integrated product lineage comes out. Everything in between is the machinery that turns the former into the latter without ever losing the thread of why a given piece of work was done or what it was built against.\\n\\nThe input is a plan — a settled statement of intent describing what should change. The output is lineage — a durable, ordered record of the work that was actually built, verified, and integrated, each step traceable back to the intent that motivated it. The build flow is what carries a plan across that gap.\\n\\nThe structure that spans the gap is the Work Graph. A **Work Graph** is the executable, content-addressed form of a plan: the plan lowered into a dependency-ordered set of independent units of work, each pinned to exactly what it builds against and what it is expected to produce. It is neither the plan nor the lineage but the substrate between them — the thing a plan becomes once it is made buildable, and the thing every later stage reads from and writes results back into. Because it is content-addressed, each unit and each input is named by its content, so what a piece of work depends on is fixed rather than merely referenced.\\n\\nFrom that structure the flow proceeds in four stages. First, the plan is **lowered** into a Work Graph and split into independent units of work. Next, each unit is **built** on its own, producing a self-contained set of changes against a base composed from a shared starting point and the work it depends on. Those changes are then **verified** by two independent signals, so that confidence does not rest on a single check. Finally, the verified work is **integrated** as a batch into product lineage, extending the durable record that the flow exists to produce.\\n\\nThe sections that follow take each stage in turn, at the same altitude: what the stage is for, what it consumes, and what it hands to the next. The closing recap makes the outputs-to-inputs handoffs between the stages explicit, so the whole flow reads as one path from plan to lineage.\\n\\n## Lowering to a Work Graph {#el:lowering}\\n\\nLowering is the first stage: it takes an approved plan and turns it into a Work Graph. A plan states intent at the altitude of what should change; it does not, on its own, say how that intent divides into work that can be built and checked. Lowering closes that distance. It reads the plan and resolves it into the dependency-ordered set of independent units the Work Graph is made of, deciding both what each unit covers and which other units it must build against.\\n\\nThe unit lowering produces is a packet. A **packet** is a single independent unit of work in the Work Graph: a bounded slice of the plan with its own purpose, its own declared set of surfaces it is allowed to touch, and its own list of the packets it depends on. A packet is small enough to build and verify on its own, yet self-describing enough that nothing outside it needs to be consulted to know what it is responsible for. The dependencies a packet declares are what order the graph; the surfaces it declares are what keep two packets from silently writing over each other.\\n\\nLowering hands the next stage a complete graph of these packets — every unit of work the plan implies, each pinned to what it depends on and scoped to what it may change. Nothing has been built yet; the stage's whole job is to make the plan buildable.\\n\\n### Packetization {#el:packetization}\\n\\nPacketization is the part of lowering that decides the packets themselves — where one unit of work ends and the next begins. **Packetization** is the division of a plan into packets: choosing the boundaries so that each packet is independently buildable, its write scope does not overlap another's, and the dependencies between packets form an order that can actually be followed. It is the judgment inside lowering that determines how coarse or fine the units are.\\n\\nGood packetization pulls in two directions at once. Boundaries drawn too coarsely produce packets that cannot be built or verified without dragging in unrelated work; drawn too finely, they multiply dependencies until the order dominates the work. Packetization settles those boundaries so the resulting graph is both a faithful decomposition of the plan and an order the later stages can execute one packet at a time.\\n\\n## Per-Packet Change Sets {#el:change-sets}\\n\\nOnce the graph exists, the flow builds it one packet at a time, and each build produces a Change Set. A **Change Set** is the self-contained result of building a single packet: the full set of changes that packet makes to its declared surfaces, expressed as complete new content rather than as a bundle of edits against something the reader must reconstruct. It is what a packet is when it has been built — the packet's declared intent turned into concrete, reviewable changes, and nothing beyond the surfaces that packet was scoped to touch. Each Change Set records both the base it was built against and the changes it lays down, so it is never adrift from the state it assumes.\\n\\nBuilding per packet keeps each unit of work honest to its scope. A Change Set carries only its own packet's changes, so it can be read, verified, and integrated as one coherent thing without untangling it from the rest of the flow. The two subsections below cover the two ideas that make per-packet building work: which packet is built next, and what it is built against.\\n\\n### The Dependency Frontier {#el:dependency-frontier}\\n\\nThe order in which packets are built is governed by the dependency frontier. The **dependency frontier** is the set of packets whose dependencies have all been built but which have not yet been built themselves — the graph's current edge of ready work. A packet sits on the frontier exactly when everything it declared a dependency on already exists as a built Change Set, and not before. A packet that declares no dependencies is on the frontier from the start, since it has nothing to wait for.\\n\\nThe frontier is what makes the graph executable without a fixed schedule. Building proceeds by taking packets off the frontier; each Change Set that completes may satisfy the last outstanding dependency of packets further along, moving them onto the frontier in turn. The stage advances by consuming the frontier until no packets remain, always building only work whose inputs are already in hand.\\n\\n### Composed Bases {#el:composed-bases}\\n\\nA packet is not built directly against the plan; it is built against a composed base. A **composed base** is the base a packet builds against, assembled by layering the Change Sets of exactly the packets it depends on onto the graph's pinned base — the shared starting state, drawn from existing product lineage, that every packet build begins from beneath its dependencies. It is the state of the surfaces as that pinned base and those dependencies together have left them — the specific, dependency-determined ground on which this packet's own changes are laid down. A packet with no dependencies builds directly against the pinned base alone; each packet that does have dependencies layers their Change Sets on top of that same base, so the pinned base is a first-class input to every build rather than something only root packets see.\\n\\nComposing the base from the pinned base plus just the declared dependencies is what lets independent packets build in parallel without interfering. Each packet sees precisely the shared starting state plus the work it was defined to build on, so its Change Set is meaningful against a known state rather than against whatever happened to be present. Because the Work Graph is content-addressed, a composed base is fixed by the content of the pinned base and of the dependencies layered onto it: the same base and the same dependencies compose the same ground every time.\\n\\n## Dual-Signal Verification {#el:dual-signal-verification}\\n\\nVerification is the stage that decides whether a built Change Set is fit to integrate, and it does so with more than one check. **Dual-signal verification** is the practice of gating each Change Set on two independent signals of correctness, requiring both to clear it before the work is allowed to advance. It is not a single test read twice, and it is not two views of the same evidence; it is two separate lines of evidence about the same changes, each capable of catching a fault the other misses.\\n\\nThe load-bearing property is that the two signals are independent. **Two independent signals** are two checks that draw their confidence from different sources, so that a fault which fools one has no reason to fool the other. Independence is what the whole stage rests on: two checks that share an origin share its blind spots, so agreement between them says little, whereas agreement between signals with unrelated failure modes is real corroboration. A Change Set passes verification only when both signals clear it; a disagreement between them is itself information, marking work that looks right by one measure but not the other and holding it back rather than letting it through. Because confidence rests on two sources rather than one, a single blind spot does not become a silent path to integration.\\n\\nVerification consumes the Change Sets that per-packet building produced and hands the next stage only those both signals agree on. It neither builds nor integrates; its whole job is to admit fit work and withhold the rest, so that what reaches the record has cleared two independent bars rather than one.\\n\\n## Batch Integration into Product Lineage {#el:batch-integration}\\n\\nThe final stage takes the verified Change Sets and folds them into the durable record. **Batch integration** is the integration of verified work as a batch — a set of Change Sets brought into the record together as one ordered step rather than one at a time — so that the record advances in coherent increments. Integrating as a batch keeps the changes that were built and verified against one another entering the record together, rather than interleaving with unrelated work in ways their verification never accounted for.\\n\\nAdmission into the batch is dependency-closed. A verified Change Set is eligible to integrate only when every Change Set it was built against — its whole chain of dependencies back to the pinned base — has itself cleared verification and is present in the same batch; a Change Set clearing its own two signals is necessary but not sufficient. When any dependency fails verification, the Change Sets built on it are withheld along with it, because each was built against a composed base that the failed dependency helped compose. This is what keeps the flow faithful to the composed-base model: nothing enters the record without the base it assumes entering too, so a dependent can never advance past a dependency that verification held back.\\n\\nWhat the batch extends is product lineage. **Product lineage** is the durable, ordered record of integrated work: each increment traceable back through the Change Set that built it, the packet that scoped it, and the plan that motivated it. Lineage is the output the whole flow exists to produce — the standing answer to what was built, in what order, and why. It is also the source of the pinned base every packet in the next graph builds from, so each integrated batch becomes the ground the following flow starts on. Batch integration is the stage that writes to it, extending the record by exactly the verified, dependency-closed work of the batch and preserving the traceability that makes lineage more than a log.\\n\\n## How the Stages Compose {#el:how-the-stages-compose}\\n\\nRead as one path, the stages hand their outputs directly to the next stage's inputs. Lowering consumes the plan and produces the Work Graph — the dependency-ordered set of packets, pinned to a base drawn from existing product lineage. Per-packet building consumes the graph a packet at a time, taking ready packets off the dependency frontier and building each against a base composed by layering its dependencies' Change Sets onto that pinned base, so the graph's output becomes each build's input. Verification consumes those Change Sets and admits only the ones two independent signals agree on. Batch integration consumes the verified Change Sets and extends product lineage with them as a batch — but only where each Change Set's dependencies cleared verification alongside it, holding back any whose base did not clear the same bar, so the record never gains a dependent without the dependency it stands on. The batch it folds in is the same lineage that supplied the pinned base, now carried one increment forward. The lineage that comes out is the plan that went in — carried across the gap, made buildable, built, checked, and recorded — with every increment still traceable to the intent that motivated it.\\n\",\n    \"docs/concepts/work-graph.md\": \"# Work Graph\\n\\nPurpose: define the Work Graph IR.\\n\\nThe L4 IR: the machine-oriented dependency graph of work packets derived from an accepted implementation plan, optimized for scheduling rather than human reading. It removes schedulability ambiguity.\\n\\nInvariants:\\n\\n- Acyclic; every packet anchored to the plan element it derives from (`derived_from`).\\n- Parallel packets have disjoint write scopes.\\n- No prose rationale — that lives at L3. The demotion is deliberate: naming the architecture after one vendor billing shape would couple the compiler to it.\\n\\n## The scheduling objective\\n\\nCapacity is a first-class scheduling input: the scheduler weighs pass requirements, backend capability declarations, capacity remaining, reset time, marginal cost, and historical success when binding lanes to backends. For resetting capacity the objective is to maximize useful engineering work while arriving near zero shortly before reset. Expiring capacity left unspent is waste; capacity spent on meaningless work is worse.\\n\\n## Harvest produces durable evidence\\n\\nExpiring capacity is converted into durable evidence through cataloged review-posture parameterizations — adversarial, falsification, second-opinion, plan-critique, test-gap, doc-freshness, dependency-audit, stale-scan, coherence. A harvest run is an ordinary `review` pass run producing an ordinary Review Ledger: pinned, attributed, gate-consumable. The harvest backlog references posture parameterizations; it may define no new passes. Harvest is never fake work — a run whose evidence nothing can consume is not scheduled.\\n\\n## Pools, snapshots, and a deterministic function\\n\\nThe accepted scheduler (RFC 0008) makes the accounting concrete. Capacity lives in **pools** — vendor quota (learned, since no vendor exposes a trustworthy remaining-quota API), local compute slots, and Principal attention, the scarcest pool of all, whose size is declared policy and never telemetry-derived. The scheduler itself is a deterministic pure function over content-addressed inputs: every binding pins the capacity snapshot and policy hashes that produced it, so \\\"why did this run there\\\" is a replayable computation, not archaeology. Harvest is a two-party protocol — the scheduler publishes an expiring-capacity budget; the Driver's harvest planner converts it into ordinary, visible plan records — and the Principal-attention pool paces producing work so expiring vendor capacity is never converted into human-attention debt.\\n\\n## Capacity never touches meaning\\n\\nCapacity pressure may never touch check gates, review gates, or claim minting (D0002.C9). A gate does not loosen because capacity is scarce; a claim does not promote because capacity was expiring. RFC 0008 enforces this by construction — gate evaluation has no parameter through which capacity state can arrive, and scheduler records carry no claim or verdict vocabulary. Capacity pressure defers *reaching* gates; it never weakens one. And because scheduler outputs are never semantic — rescheduling invalidates nothing — capacity policy evolves freely as policy commits, no RFC required, without changing what a single artifact means.\\n\\nCanonical: [RFC 0008](../../rfcs/0008-scheduler-and-capacity-policy/design.md) · [D0008](../../decisions/D0008-scheduler-and-capacity-policy.md), [RFC 0002](../../rfcs/0002-compiler-architecture/design.md) (Boundary Decision Procedure), [Scheduler (concept)](../concepts/scheduler.md), [Capacity (concept)](../concepts/capacity.md), [`policy/`](../../policy/).\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/cross-repository-compilation.md\": \"# Cross-Repository Compilation\\n\\nPurpose: explain why the compiler reaches across more than one repository the way\\nit does — and why that reach adds no new mechanism.\\n\\nThe canonical statement is the decision record\\n[D0014](../../decisions/D0014-cross-repository-compilation.md) (owning\\n[RFC 0014](../../rfcs/0014-cross-repository-compilation/design.md)). It does not.\\nEach repository keeps its own graph-of-record and its own ledger; a\\ncross-repository compilation is **linked per-repository compilations exchanging\\nrepo-qualified pins**, each admitting into its own graph under its own\\nrepository's policy. Nothing is shared but references, and references are\\ncontent-addressed. The single graph-of-record per repository (D0009.C1) survives\\nthe fleet intact, and so does everything that rested on it: provenance totality,\\ncomputed claims, and one invalidation algebra.\\n\\nThis is why cross-repository compilation is a *strengthening*, not a new\\nsubsystem. D0010.C11 (decided later)\\nforbids exactly that: admission is execution-free and content-addressed, and the\\ngate path may not make a live cross-graph read, because a gate whose outcome\\ndepends on another ledger's live timing is no longer a deterministic function of\\ncontent.\\n\\nThe **Foreign Head Attestation** resolves it. When the Driver plans a\\ncompilation that touches another repository's head, it reads that head *at\\nplanning* — off the gate path — and freezes what it saw into a local, immutable\\npiece of evidence: an Exogenous Change Record capturing the foreign\\n`{repo_id, identity, content_hash, seal_domain, as_of}`. The gate and admission\\npath then read only that local attestation. The live cross-graph read happens\\nonce, at planning, where reading the world is already the job; the gate computes\\nhashes over local content, exactly as it does for a purely local pin. D0009.C8's\\nlaziness stands — the attestation is *how* freshness is lazy at gate time — and\\nD0010.C11 holds across graphs by construction.\\n\\n## Freshness is still the one algebra\\n\\nA cross-repository pin is fresh iff the latest attestation for its foreign head\\nstill reports the pinned content hash. When the other repository's head moves, a\\nfresh attestation reporting a new hash is admitted at planning, and that head\\nmovement decays every dependent claim exactly as any head movement does — a\\nstaleness wave, the same invalidation algebra, no cross-graph event routing (a\\nhead moving in one repository never pushes marks into another; that would couple\\nledgers and fan out across the fleet). Cross-graph freshness is the local\\nalgebra over one indirection, not a second mechanism.\\n\\n## Trust is honest about where it ends\\n\\nAn attestation records the other repository's seal domain, and a cross-repository\\npin trusts that repository exactly as far as its seals warrant. Within one\\nworkstation's data-home, every graph shares the single-OS-user trust domain — so\\na same-workstation cross-repository pin is crash-evidence, just like a local pin,\\nand adds no trust surface (rung-2 per-lane uid isolation, D0012.C6, strengthens\\nthis to tamper-evidence where the deployment provisions distinct uids — see\\n[Hostile-Lane Containment](hostile-lane-containment.md)). The v1 reach is a fleet\\nunder one workstation's trust domain. The single-OS-user trust statement is not quietly\\nwidened to make the fleet look bigger than it is.\\n\\n## What integration across graphs means\\n\\nA change produced under an intent concerning one repository can be verified and\\nlinked into another repository's product lineage. Integration is the same\\ndeterministic topological linking as within one repository (D0010.C8), run\\nagainst the *target* repository's graph: its product ref moves under its own\\ngate, its ledger records the application. The producing intent lives in one\\ngraph, the integrating admission in another, and the two are bound by the\\ncross-repository pin and the attestation that resolves it. The\\nexecution-independence guard extends across graphs: no lane, adversarial or\\nmerely nondeterministic, can make a cross-repository admission depend on\\nexecution, and a forged or stale attestation resolves to *stale*, never to a\\nspurious accept.\\n\\n## Why this matters\\n\\nThe compiler's guarantees were designed for one repository and turn out to cost\\nnothing to extend to many — because \\\"many\\\" was never allowed to mean \\\"a bigger\\nshared thing.\\\" It means several sound repositories exchanging content-addressed\\nevidence. An RFC is the design conversation: rationale, alternatives, dissent. A decision record is the accepted semantic state distilled from that conversation: what is in force, its consequences, its scope of constraint. Downstream work links against decisions, never RFC prose (P8) — when you need to know what the architecture *is*, you read a decision; when you need to know *why*, you read the owning RFC.\\n\\n## Generated interfaces\\n\\nDecision records are compiled interfaces, never hand-written prose. The `decision-generation` pass produces them from the accepted heads of the owning RFC identity, pinning the exact stage hashes it generated from. A hand-edit is refused at admission — a version with no producing pass run cannot enter the graph (W4). And the Principal accepts every generation and regeneration: generation without acceptance would make the compiler the author of its own constitution.\\n\\n## Element grain\\n\\nRecords carry element structure — decision clauses with stable anchors — from day one. Consumers link against clauses, not documents, via `constrained_by` edges. When a regeneration changes clause C3 and leaves C7 intact, only the consumers of C3 go stale. Element grain is what keeps architectural memory from becoming an invalidation bomb: the constitution can evolve without re-proving the world.\\n\\n## Graceful staleness, hard revocation\\n\\nWhen an owning RFC's accepted head moves, its decision record goes stale and regeneration is mandatory — but consumers may keep linking against the last-accepted version while regeneration is pending. Each such run appends a deviation warning: visible, bounded, honest. Only **revocation** — an explicit acceptance-authority act — fails closed.\\n\\nThe distinction is deliberate. Stale means \\\"unproven against the present\\\"; revoked means \\\"no longer permitted.\\\" A compiler that failed closed on every staleness would deadlock itself on ordinary evolution; one that shrugged at revocation would have no constitution at all.\\n\\n## Constitutional scope\\n\\nThe runtime wave fixed where decisions live and how far they reach (RFC 0009). **Constitutional decisions** — what the compiler *is* — belong to the compiler repository's own graph, the graph every other graph names as its core at genesis; pass contracts resolve them there at run time through ordinary repo-qualified pins, with ordinary staleness semantics, so the constitution is read from where it is decided rather than copied into binaries or per-repository trees. Repository-local decisions constrain only their own graph. If the core graph is unregistered or a required constitutional record is revoked, the Driver refuses to plan — fail-closed exactly and only where revocation already fails closed.\\n\\n## Admission completeness\\n\\nA decision record is one of three projections a fully admitted capability leaves in the graph. The implementation is Product Artifacts; the justification is the decision record; the explanation is canonical documentation — itself a Product Artifact, not commentary that trails the change. P11 binds the three: code whose decision or documentation is missing is not admitted architecture, however real the diff. Implementation never silently outruns explanation, because the gap is a computed fact of the graph rather than an informal backlog. The computed form is the target state `capability-admission-complete`; its honest v1 bound and strengthening path live in the catalog entry.\\n\\nCanonical: [`decisions/index.md`](../../decisions/index.md), [RFC 0003, Decision Role](../../rfcs/0003-intermediate-representations/design.md), [RFC 0005, Decision-Record Semantics](../../rfcs/0005-artifact-lifecycle-and-state-machine/design.md), [RFC 0009, Constitutional Decisions](../../rfcs/0009-provenance-ledger-and-artifact-store/design.md), [Decision Record (concept)](../concepts/decision-record.md).\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/discoveries.md\": \"# Discoveries\\n\\n\\u003e This document is not normative.\\n\\u003e\\n\\u003e It exists to preserve architectural discoveries that changed the direction\\n\\u003e of the compiler.\\n\\u003e\\n\\u003e Read it before major architecture work.\\n\\u003e\\n\\u003e Do not treat its contents as accepted truth. validated live by `dogfood-ready@1` (ledger seq 1280).*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0014 — Self-Hosting Begins with the Constitution\\n\\nThe first successful self-improvement was not code generation.\\n\\nIt was constitutional amendment.\\n\\nThe compiler upgraded its own amendment machinery before using it to amend the constitution.\\n\\nThe compiler protected its own invariants before allowing itself to evolve.\\n\\nThat moment marked the beginning of genuine self-hosting.\\n\\n*Historical note: the machinery it describes is D0011 and the decision-generation retrofit of the constitution (D0001.C12).*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0015 — Strengthen Before You Extend\\n\\nA recurring pattern emerged.\\n\\nInstead of introducing new concepts, the compiler repeatedly strengthened existing ones.\\n\\nExamples include:\\n\\n- execution backend instead of model taxonomy\\n- documentation as Product Artifact instead of new artifact type\\n- capability admission as constitutional invariant instead of a new gate\\n- scheduler policy instead of semantic scheduling\\n\\nArchitectural maturity appeared as subtraction rather than accumulation.\\n\\n*Absorbed: N11 / D0001.C12.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0016 — The Compiler Protects Meaning\\n\\nThe compiler does not merely preserve code.\\n\\nIt preserves semantics.\\n\\nWhen explanations diverge from constitutional meaning, the compiler treats that as an architectural inconsistency rather than documentation drift.\\n\\nMeaning becomes another invariant.\\n\\n*Absorbed in part: P11 and RFC 0001's never-diverges rendering contract. The broader claim still floats.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0017 — The Compiler Compiles Subjects, Not Repositories\\n\\nThe compiler does not fundamentally compile repositories.\\n\\nIt compiles subjects with desired state.\\n\\nA repository is one kind of subject.\\n\\nA workstation is another.\\n\\nThe realization emerged while planning the retirement of the bootstrap compiler.\\n\\nRetiring it was not a change to the compiler. It was a change to the workstation's desired state — the teardown belongs to the host's own graph, and the compiler's graph merely observes the event.\\n\\nThe request grammar had already noticed: a compilation request names a subject and a target state. Nothing in it names a repository.\\n\\nThe architectural consequence is ownership.\\n\\nEach subject owns exactly one artifact graph.\\n\\nCompiler changes belong to the compiler's graph.\\n\\nRepository evolution belongs to the repository's graph.\\n\\nHost posture belongs to the host's graph.\\n\\nOther graphs observe those changes through evidence, never through shared ownership.\\n\\n*Absorbed in part: for repository subjects — D0009.C1 (one graph-of-record per repository) and D0014.C1/C2 (no cross-repository graph, no shared mutable store; foreign change enters a graph only as an admitted Foreign Head Attestation: observation through evidence). The generalization to non-repository subjects still floats.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0018 — The Cost of a Noun\\n\\nEvery new noun is a commitment to an ontology.\\n\\nA noun must justify its lifetime cost: definition, ownership, invariants, lifecycle, documentation, teaching, and maintenance.\\n\\nTherefore the first question is never \\\"What should we call this?\\\"\\n\\nIt is: \\\"Can the existing ubiquitous language already express it?\\\"\\n\\n*Absorbed: N8 (a term enters only through an explicit Language Amendment), N11 / D0001.C12 (strengthen before extend), and P2 (every admitted noun gets exactly one home, never shadowing another). Discovery 0015 records the resulting pattern; this records its price.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0019 — The Instance Is Not the Product\\n\\nA compiler instance is not part of the compiler product.\\n\\nIt is evidence that the product compiled something.\\n\\nThe compiler is a product.\\n\\nA compilation is an instance.\\n\\nThe product defines the compiler — language, decisions, runtime, schemas, policies, explanations, declarations — and ships.\\n\\nThe instance describes one execution — plan logs, handoffs, pass narratives, deep reviews, satisfied one-shot target states, observations, migration history — and belongs to the instance.\\n\\nSelf-hosting hid the cut: when the compiler compiles itself, the subject's diary and the product's sources share one working tree, and instance evidence masquerades as product content. The fleet perspective exposed it; the ownership rule makes it principled.\\n\\nThe division is safe by construction: P11 already required every admitted capability to carry its product projections — implementation, decision record, explanation — so the instance material was always scaffolding.\\n\\n*Absorbed in part: D0009 (the ledger is the instance's memory; records are not artifacts), P11 (the product projections that make scaffolding removable), and Discovery 0017 (one graph per subject). Still floats: the division is not yet enacted — the product tree carries one instance's evidence, a visible consequence of self-hosting (D0011) that the fleet (D0014) newly exposes.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Discovery 0020 — Knowledge Is Neither Product Nor Instance\\n\\nThe compiler learns, and what it learns is neither the product nor the instance.\\n\\nA lesson — a backend's failure mode, a verification pattern, a discovered invariant, a simplification of the language — is not a source, a decision, a schema, or a declaration, so it is not the product.\\n\\nNor is it the instance: an instance is evidence that the product compiled *one* subject, and a lesson is true across many. No single instance owns it.\\n\\nDiscovery 0019 cut the instance from the product. This is the cut it implied — a third thing, distilled across instances, owned by the fleet.\\n\\nToday that thing has no home. It lives only while a context window or a human still holds it: accumulated as notes and prompt cargo, gone when the window closes. The compiler that computes truth for everyone forgets what it learns, and rediscovers it subject after subject.\\n\\nThe name says why it is neither: knowledge is *compiled*, not held. Derived from the evidence many instances leave; promoted only when that evidence is sufficient and independent; decaying when superseded — the claim model's dynamics, turned on content the claim model does not carry. It is not a Claim (a claim is a contentless level over one artifact version). It is not any evidence kind the ontology has (each binds a single target). It is the fleet's own memory — and the fleet has never had one.\\n\\n*Absorbed: nothing yet — this floats by construction, as its predecessors did before enactment. It resolves two standing floats: Discovery 0017's generalization to non-repository subjects (the fleet-knowledge subject is one), and Discovery 0019's placement of all observations on the instance side with no promotion path out. It borrows the claim dynamics (RFC 0005 — leveled, evidence-bound, decaying, independence) without being a Claim: a lesson's trust is the computed claim level over knowledge that is the fleet-knowledge subject's own **Product Artifact** — not a Claim, and not a new evidence kind. It pays the Cost of a Noun (Discovery 0018) at the floor: Evidence keeps its four kinds exactly, and the whole design is one new subject and one new knowledge-promotion pass, sourcing the fleet's existing evidence through the existing Foreign Head Attestation (D0014). That single pass — and the RFC that earns it — is the next advance.*\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Open Question\\n\\nHow many additional discoveries remain before the compiler begins discovering them without human prompting?\\n\\nThat question is intentionally left unanswered.\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/driver.md\": \"# The Driver Is a Program\\n\\nPurpose: explain why the compiler driver is a deterministic program, not an agent.\\n\\nRetired alias: this component was formerly the Meta-Operator (RFC 0001, Retired Terms).\\n\\n## Why a program\\n\\nThe Driver advances artifacts toward requested target states. Everything it does is mechanical: read the graph, evaluate the target predicate, plan the pass sequence that satisfies the unmet conjuncts, request scheduling, evaluate gates over submitted results, admit, append provenance, repeat. Planning is graph reachability over declared catalog data — pass contracts declare what consumes and produces what, so the path from current state to target is computable, not judged.\\n\\nIf the Driver ever \\\"needs judgment,\\\" a gate or a declaration is underspecified; the fix is the declaration, not a smarter Driver. This is the structural defense against the manager-agent failure mode: a Driver that improvises cannot be replayed, audited, or trusted at the admission boundary. Judgment exists in the system — it lives in review passes and acceptance gates, where it is recorded, bounded, and attributable.\\n\\n## What it owns\\n\\nArtifact state inspection. Target-predicate evaluation. Pass planning. Scheduler invocation. Gate evaluation and admission. Staleness propagation, revalidation scheduling, and re-stamping. Escalation.\\n\\n## What it never owns\\n\\nEngineering work. Artifact content — it produces no artifacts, ever; every output is a ledger record (P1). Gate overrides. Direct backend conversation: backends submit, the Driver admits. Architecture synthesis, implementation, review, verification — those are compiler passes, executed in lanes.\\n\\n## An invoked program, not a resident one\\n\\nThe runtime foundation (RFC 0006) made the program claim physical: there is no daemon, and no process whose uptime is a truth condition. The Driver runs as **drive sessions** — invocation to quiescence — serialized per repository graph by the Graph Store's drive lease, prompted by non-authoritative wakes, and replayable from pinned inputs: same graph, ledger, catalog, and policy produce the same decisions. Why the daemon is gone for good: [No-Daemon Runtime](no-daemon-runtime.md).\\n\\n## Plans are ledger records\\n\\nA Driver plan is not an artifact; it is a plan record appended to the provenance ledger. This keeps the subject layer clean — nothing the Driver emits can be pinned, gated, or claimed against — and makes planning fully auditable after the fact. Planning may read provenance as data (retry counts, failure history) to break livelock; gates and acceptance never read provenance for authority.\\n\\n## Escalation is the only interruptive act\\n\\nWhen compilation cannot proceed without the Principal, the Driver appends an escalation record with a closed reason code — eight codes since the Epoch 2 amendment: `ambiguous_goal`, `missing_authority`, `contradicting_decisions`, `committee_stalemate`, `override_required`, `bounds_exhausted`, `binding_unsatisfiable`, `independence_unsatisfiable` — and the affected subgraph halts. Resolution is an appended authority event. The Driver never nags, never improvises around a block, never proceeds on assumption.\\n\\nCanonical: [RFC 0002, Driver](../../rfcs/0002-compiler-architecture/design.md); [RFC 0006](../../rfcs/0006-driver-control-surface/design.md); [Driver (concept)](../concepts/driver.md).\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/fleet-catalog-resolution.md\": \"# Fleet Catalog Resolution\\n\\nPurpose: explain why a fleet repository's drive resolves a *merged* catalog after the product/instance division, and why this is a loader delivery rather than a new architectural rule.\\n\\n## The gap the division opened\\n\\n`product-instance-divided@1` (Discovery 0019 — the instance is not the product) moved every foreign-subject target-state predicate out of the product catalog and into the instance repository. That is exactly right for the compiler's own graph: striatum-next drives against the generic lifecycle and standing-capability predicates, all of which stay in the product catalog beside the structural vocabulary (passes, gates, artifact-kinds, IRs, pipelines). The compiler's own drive never named a foreign target-state, so the division never had to say how a foreign target-state would be found.\\n\\nA *fleet* repository does name them. Praxis's `reminder-bot-product`, `frontier-verified`, and their kin describe praxis compilations; under Discovery 0019 they are instance evidence and live in the instance catalog (`striatum-instance/striatum-next/catalog/target-states/`). But the compiler that drives praxis loads its vocabulary from a single root, and after the division no single root is whole:\\n\\n- The **product** root carries the structural vocabulary and the generic states, but not praxis's foreign target-state — a request for it is an unknown target.\\n- The **instance** root carries the foreign target-state, but no `passes/` — a load of it errors on the missing subdirectory.\\n\\nNeither root alone resolves. The division split the vocabulary along an ownership cut that is correct for durability but that no loader knew how to re-join at drive time.\\n\\n## Why it is delivery, not a decision\\n\\nThe catalog model (RFC 0001/0005) fixes what the vocabulary *means* — a target-state is a versioned predicate over the artifact graph; a pass is a versioned transformation contract — but it never fixed the vocabulary's on-disk *arity*. A catalog assembled from a base directory plus overlay directories is the same catalog, with the same semantics, as one assembled from a single directory. Overlaying changes how the loader reads the vocabulary off disk; it changes nothing about the vocabulary. So this closes the gap by delivery under P2/N11 — no RFC clause is amended, no new durable concept is introduced.\\n\\nThe composition is not arbitrary. D0011.C1 makes the core graph another graph's pinned environment: the shipped compiler product *is* the fleet repository's environment. So the product catalog is the natural **base**, and the fleet's own foreign target-states — its instance's contribution — are the **overlay** layered on top. The direction of layering falls straight out of the ownership relation the division already established.\\n\\n## The shape\\n\\n`LoadCatalog(root, overlays...)` reads the base root exactly as before — the full structural and generic vocabulary — then, for each overlay root in order, layers its `target-states/` on top. Three properties make the merge safe and honest:\\n\\n- **Overlays contribute target-states only.** An overlay carries no passes, gates, or kinds; the structural vocabulary has exactly one home, the base. This keeps the ownership cut sharp — an instance never redefines a pass — and it is why an overlay's absent `target-states/` subdirectory is tolerated rather than an error: an overlay may legitimately carry none.\\n- **Later overlay wins, deterministically.** On a target-state id collision the last overlay in flag order wins, in the order given. Precedence is explicit and reproducible; catalog maps stay stably iterated.\\n- **No overlays is byte-identical to today.** A drive that names no overlay loads exactly the base catalog the shipped compiler loads standalone. The non-fleet path does not change — the guard test pins this alongside the resolution property.\\n\\nAt the CLI, `-catalog-overlay` is a repeatable flag layered over `-catalog`. Because a fleet drive dispatches lanes and wakes itself after commit from a detached supervisor with an unrelated working directory, `wakeCommand` re-emits each overlay as an absolute path — the post-commit wake resolves the same merged catalog the session did, or the foreign state in flight would vanish under the wake.\\n\\n## What it is worth\\n\\nThe mechanical substance is a standing guard: a base catalog overlaid with a foreign target-state resolves that state while the base-only load never gains it, later-overlay-wins holds, and a structurally-partial overlay is tolerated. That guard plus the pass-bracket floor is the honest evaluation bound of `fleet-catalog-resolution@1`. This is a loader-shape delivery; it does not route itself through the Dual-Signal funnel, so it closes at the floor — `Asserted`, honestly. Earning `Verified` for a change like this is what `evolution-earns-verified` names, through the compiler's own funnel; it is not smuggled in here.\\n\\nThe division made the catalog durable by cutting it in two. This makes it *usable* by a fleet repository again, by teaching the loader to re-join the halves at drive time along the same ownership seam the division cut.\\n\\n## Registration-derived resolution (`fleet-catalog-resolution@2`)\\n\\nThe v1 seam left one thing hand-passed: someone had to know where the instance lives and say `-catalog-overlay` on every invocation. `@2` moves that knowledge to where it already belonged — the repository's registration. A registered repository's workstation-registry entry may declare, under `resolution.instance_catalog_overlay`, the single overlay root of its instance catalog. This is repository policy the driver reads, never compiler semantics: nothing about what a catalog *means* changed, only where the driver learns which overlay to compose. A registry written before the declaration existed decodes unchanged — the key is optional and absent by default.\\n\\nResolution happens once per invocation, at the session-construction seam — after the graph opens (so the repository is named by its registered identity) and before the catalog loads. The rules, in force order:\\n\\n- **Explicit flags override.** Any `-catalog-overlay` on the invocation is the effective list, exactly as given, in flag order; registration is not consulted. Override, never append — an operator who names overlays gets precisely those.\\n- **Registration derives.** With no flag, a declared `instance_catalog_overlay` becomes the single-element effective list: a plain `striatum -repo \\u003cfleet\\u003e drive` resolves the merged catalog with nothing hand-passed.\\n- **Absence is silence.** A repository declaring nothing loads the base catalog exactly as before — the non-fleet drive is byte-identical to the pre-declaration one.\\n- **A used declaration must be usable.** The declared root must be an absolute, clean path naming an existing readable directory; a violation — like a registry that cannot be read at the resolution point — refuses the invocation *before* any catalog load, as a registration-resolution failure naming the repository and the offending path. The failure is configuration, surfaced near its cause, never a degraded catalog. A valid root without `target-states/` remains v1's tolerated empty overlay; the composition semantics above are untouched.\\n- **The wake receives a snapshot.** The effective list is re-emitted to the post-commit wake and the standing liveness timer as explicit absolute `-catalog-overlay` argv, so a wake resolves the same merged catalog its session did — through the flags-override branch, by construction. A wake never re-reads registration; a declaration edited mid-flight changes the next fresh session, not a wake already armed.\\n\\nEvery verb that opens graph and catalog resolves the same way — `drive`, `status`, `accept`, and kin all see one merged catalog for a registered fleet repository; this is session construction, not a drive special case. The authoring surface stays deliberately thin: no CLI verb writes the declaration yet, so the v1 authoring path is a direct edit of the workstation `registry.json` — a `striatum` setter verb is a new surface decision, not smuggled in here.\\n\\n## Companion: a fleet repository's checks resolve to the repository too (`checks-resolve-to-repo@1`)\\n\\nCatalog resolution is one half of a single property — *a fleet repository is compiled and verified on its own terms.* Resolving the catalog said **what target states a fleet repository can name**; it says nothing about **what teeth bite its change-sets.** That is the check registry, and it had the same latent defect one layer down.\\n\\nThe check registry is per-repo policy (RFC 0010): a content-addressed set of checks resident in the repository's own tree at `policy/checks/repository.json`, describing that repository's verification. But the `-checks` flag resolved its relative path against the *process working directory*, not `-repo`. On the compiler's self-drive the two coincide — the working directory *is* the target repository — so the defect was invisible. It surfaces the moment the compiler drives a foreign repository from its own directory: it looks for the registry under its own tree, finds its own registry or none, and verifies the fleet repository's change-sets on the compiler's terms. A fleet drive could resolve praxis's target states while still gating them on striatum-next's Go checks — exactly the language-hardwiring `praxis-earns-verified` fought, resurfacing at the path-resolution layer.\\n\\nThe fix is symmetric with catalog resolution and just as small: a relative `-checks` resolves against `-repo`, so the registry a drive loads is the one in the target repository's tree. An absolute `-checks` is an explicit override, honored as given. The self-drive, where `-repo` defaults to the working directory, resolves to the same file it always did — byte-identical. And because a fleet drive wakes itself after commit from a detached supervisor with an unrelated working directory, the resolution runs once at session build and the wake re-emits the already-repo-relative path (absolutized), so the wake never re-resolves the registry against the supervisor's directory.\\n\\nLike catalog resolution, this is delivery, not a decision: the check model already fixes the registry as per-repo policy resident in the repository's tree; resolving its path relative to the repository it belongs to is fixing *where the loader looks*, not changing *what a check means* (P2/N11, no clause amended). The two halves converge on a single shape — registration. The catalog half arrived at `fleet-catalog-resolution@2` above: the registration's `resolution` object now derives the overlay. The check half arrived at `checks-resolve-to-repo@2`: the same `resolution` object carries a `check_registry` sibling, and a registered fleet repository's check registry auto-resolves from it — a plain `striatum -repo \\u003cfleet\\u003e drive` gates on the fleet repo's own checks with no hand-passed `-checks`. Both halves now share one precedence rule (an explicit flag overrides and registration is never consulted — for `-checks`, explicitness is a parse-time fact, so passing the default string or the empty string is explicit too; declaring nothing is byte-identical silence), one refusal shape (a declared-but-unusable value refuses before anything loads, as a registration-resolution failure naming the repository and the offending path — for checks, the declared path must be an absolute, clean path to an existing readable regular file), and one wake-pinning discipline (the effective decision is re-emitted verbatim to every wake surface — for checks, including the *empty* decision, pinned as an explicit empty `-checks` and rendered in the timer unit as systemd's literal `\\\"\\\"` — so a wake never re-reads registration).\\n\\nTwo structural differences distinguish the check half, both deliberate. First, the field is pointer-shaped: absent and present-empty are distinct states — a registry that never declares saves byte-identically to the pre-declaration shape, while a declared-empty `check_registry` is a declaration, refused at the point of use like every other unusable declared value. Second, refusal reach on `accept`/`reject`: checks resolution sits in `buildSession` (the session-construction seam), not in the graph-and-catalog opening the recording path calls, so a broken `check_registry` declaration never blocks recording a verdict — the bounded transition is silently skipped under its standing best-effort contract, no session (and so no weakened drive) ever comes into being, and the loud refusal arrives on the next session-constructing invocation. A broken *overlay* declaration, by contrast, refuses `accept`/`reject` before the ledger mutation, because the catalog is a genuine input of recording. The asymmetry follows the seam placement; strengthening the loudness is a registered deferral (`docs/reference/deferrals.md`).\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/hostile-lane-containment.md\": \"# Hostile-Lane Containment\\n\\nPurpose: explain why a hostile execution lane cannot corrupt what the compiler\\nadmits — and why containment is a *fence the artifact is held to* plus a\\n*delivered trust rung*, not a bigger checker.\\n\\nThe canonical statement is the decision record\\n[D0012](../../decisions/D0012-runtime-hardening.md) (owning\\n[RFC 0012](../../rfcs/0012-runtime-hardening/design.md)), whose C6 records rung-2\\nper-lane uid isolation moving from designed to delivered. This page explains the\\nshape; it does not restate the contract.\\n\\n## The theorem was relative\\n\\nCompiler soundness is independent of execution behaviour: admission is a\\ndeterministic, execution-free function of content (D0010.C1/C4), so a\\nnondeterministic — or malicious — lane cannot make the compiler admit an invalid\\nartifact. But that reduction was always stated *relative* to two things: the\\ncompleteness of the gates' checks, and the seal/trust boundary. The second half\\nwas the honest catch. A lane inside the trust domain does not corrupt the\\nadmission function; it *forges content* — it produces a submission and seals it\\nas though it were authorized work. Whether that forgery admits depends not on the\\nexecution-free core but on whether the seal/trust boundary is real.\\n\\nIn v1 that boundary was an assumption, not a proof. Every lane ran under one OS\\nuser, so keyed seals (rung 1) were *crash-evidence* — they catch an accidental\\nplain seal, but a co-resident lane could read another backend's key and seal\\nunder it. The theorem held \\\"relative to a single trusted OS user,\\\" and that\\nclause was doing real work.\\n\\n## Containment is a fence, not a distance to close\\n\\nHostile-lane containment is modelled the same way as execution-independence: not\\nas a target state with a gap to close, but as a **standing property the artifact\\nmust keep** — membership in the premises to preserve. The compiler does not\\n\\\"advance toward\\\" not-admitting-forgeries; it must *never* admit them, on every\\ncommit. So the property lives as a guard in the soundness fence family\\n(`internal/driver/soundness_guard_test.go`): a lane that seals a submission under\\na key it was not authorized to hold is refused at drain (`seal_invalid`) and\\nnever admits, however well-formed its change-set — while an authorized seal does\\nadmit, so the fence discriminates forgery from legitimate work rather than\\nrefusing everything.\\n\\nThat fence holds on *every* deployment, single-uid included. It is the admission\\nconsequence of the seal/trust boundary, and it is what stops a forged seal from\\nbecoming an accepted head.\\n\\n## The delivered rung: credentials, never contracts\\n\\nA fence that merely *detects* an unauthorized seal is not yet tamper-evidence,\\nbecause under one uid a hostile lane can still read the trusted key and produce a\\nseal that verifies. What turns detection into tamper-evidence is rung 2: each\\nlane's runtime runs under a dedicated uid that cannot read another lane's Runtime\\nSeal Key or write another lane's spool subtree. Then a hostile lane cannot even\\n*reach* the material it would need to forge.\\n\\nThe delivery is credentials and ownership only (D0012.C4) — no seam, no contract,\\nno record change; adapters stay crash-only, ledger-illiterate, A1–A8-conformant.\\nThe one design subtlety is fate-sharing. Supervision binds a runtime's whole\\nprocess tree to its Lane Supervisor through a cgroup whose init helper carries a\\nparent-death signal (D0013.C10); if the runtime dropped uid *and took the kill\\ndomain with it*, an isolated lane could outlive its supervisor. So only the\\nruntime drops — the grandchild — while the init helper stays at the supervisor's\\nuid, holding the cgroup. `cgroup.kill` reaps the runtime whatever uid it runs\\nunder, and the drop is a clone credential, not a setuid binary on the lane path.\\nIsolation changes who the runtime *is*, not how it dies.\\n\\nLane credentials are a workstation secret, resolved like seal keys — outside\\nevery repository, never in a ledger record or a backend declaration. The semantic\\nledger is byte-identical whether or not isolation is enabled (the seal-neutrality\\ndiscipline, extended from seal bytes to uids), so turning rung 2 on is a\\ndeployment switch with zero schema, corpus, or contract churn.\\n\\n## Trust stays honest about the rung it delivers\\n\\nEnforcement needs privilege: dropping to a foreign uid requires `CAP_SETUID`, and\\nthis host denies unprivileged user namespaces. So the honest statement is\\nper-deployment. Where distinct per-lane uids are provisioned, the rung-1 keyed\\nseals become tamper-evidence within the workstation, and D0010.C11's reduction\\nnarrows from \\\"relative to a single trusted OS user\\\" to \\\"relative to the checks\\nand an enforced seal/trust boundary.\\\" Where they are not — a single uid, or an\\nunprivileged host — the drop *fails closed*: a lane told to drop to a uid it\\ncannot assume never runs, never silently retaining the caller's uid, and the\\nseals honestly remain crash-evidence. Nothing in force claims a rung the\\ndeployment does not deliver (D0012.C1/C5). Cross-*workstation* trust and external\\nanchoring (rung 3) remain deferred.\\n\\n## Why a fence beats a bigger checker\\n\\nThe tempting alternative — make admission smarter, teach it to detect hostile\\noutput — would have moved trust *into* the execution-free core and made soundness\\ndepend on out-guessing an adversary. Containment does the opposite. It keeps the\\ncore dumb and deterministic, fences the one boundary the theorem was relative to,\\nand closes the relativization by *credentials* — a property of how work is\\nstarted, not of how cleverly it is inspected. The compiler does not need to\\nrecognize a hostile lane. It needs a lane to be unable to forge what it was not\\nauthorized to produce, and to be contained when it tries.\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/index.md\": \"# Explanation\\n\\nPurpose: explain why lane is not a backend\\n\\nAn earlier framing equated lanes with execution backends; this page's former name encoded that category error. A **lane** is an isolated execution context inside a pass run — an instance with a role, a write scope, and independence constraints. An **execution backend** is the adapter that launches agent runtimes into lanes. One is a place where work happens; the other is machinery that fills it.\\n\\n## The chain\\n\\n```text\\npass contract   declares lane requirements\\npass run        instantiates lanes\\nscheduler       binds lanes to execution backends (lane bindings — dispatch records)\\nbackend         launches an agent runtime into each bound lane\\n```\\n\\nLane topology — divergent lanes plus a synthesizer, review panels — is pass implementation, not contract, with one exception: contracts declare `synthesis: single | synthesized-from-N` because it affects independence accounting. Lane attribution is always recorded in provenance; the anti-aliasing condition on Verified is evaluated over it.\\n\\n## The submit/admit seam\\n\\nBackends submit; the Driver admits through gates. Nothing a backend does is true until admitted into the artifact store. The single-writer property lives at the admission boundary — which is exactly what lets execution be arbitrarily parallel and untrusted below it. Partial submission is handled per-output under the Partial-Admission Closure Rule: finished lanes' work is never discarded; the residual is re-dispatched.\\n\\nThe runtime wave (RFC 0007) made the seam physical: everything that crosses it is a content-addressed file tree in a non-authoritative spool, and the sole commit point is one atomic rename. A dispatch delivered by pipe or socket dies with the process that received it; a file tree survives the crash of both sides, and a half-written workspace that never reaches the rename simply never happened. \\\"Result or nothing\\\" is not a discipline; it is the only observable behavior the seam permits.\\n\\n## Crash-only doctrine\\n\\nBackends are crash-only: sealed work in; results and evidence out, or nothing. All supervision, liveness, and process mechanics are internal and invisible above the seam. A dead backend is indistinguishable from a slow one, and both are handled by re-dispatch — pass purity makes this safe. Abandonment is not an error state to repair; the packet is simply still unexecuted.\\n\\nTwo Epoch 2 sharpenings keep that honest under load (RFCs 0006/0007/0010). Abandonment is a *provisional* adjudication, not a death certificate: a late submission against an abandoned run is still admitted, because the backend may have been slow, not dead — the first admitted valid result wins across attempts, and a surplus result is recorded as redundant, never silently discarded. And re-dispatch is closure-then-new-run only: the prior run closes, a new run opens with the identical sealed manifest at attempt+1. No lease, heartbeat, or liveness vocabulary exists above the seam, and none may be introduced.\\n\\n## Capability is data, not semantics\\n\\nWhich backend can run a pass, how large its context is, how it prices and paces, how well it reviews versus implements — all of it is *vendor behavior*, and vendor behavior is data. It enters the compiler exactly once, as **declared capability facts** in a backend's declaration (`backends/`), and it is read exactly once, by **declared placement and independence rules** in scheduler policy (`policy/`). It never becomes compiler semantics. The reason is durability under change: frontier models turn over on a timescale of weeks, but the artifact model, the pass contracts, and the invalidation algebra must not. Anything that would have to be re-decided when a vendor ships a new model is, by construction, kept out of the layer that cannot afford to be re-decided. This is why there is no home for \\\"which model is best\\\" anywhere in the compiler — the question is real, but it is a scheduling question answered by data, not an architectural one answered by semantics.\\n\\nThe same fact therefore lives at three altitudes, and the architecture is careful about which is which. A declaration states a **prior** — a vendor-stated starting estimate carried with its own provenance and freshness horizon (`basis`, `as_of`, `review_by`), so the graph knows a latency or aliasing fact is an assumption with an expiry, not a measurement. Policy turns priors into **preference** — ordered placement rules that may re-rank or restrict, never relax anything gate-adjacent. And measured **telemetry** supersedes both, along the standing evolution gradient (D0008.C9): declarative heuristics → repository policy → telemetry-informed → self-tuning, under one invariant that never moves — *never semantic*. A scheduler that learns a backend is slower than its declaration claimed re-prefers around it; it can never thereby unlock a placement a pass contract forbids. Capability data is how the scheduler gets *better*; it is structurally incapable of making the compiler mean something *different*. When a new frontier environment appears, it is onboarded by adding a declaration and letting telemetry correct its priors — no RFC, no decision record, no touch to compiler semantics.\\n\\nCanonical: [Lane](../concepts/lane.md), [Execution Backend](../concepts/execution-backend.md), [Agent Runtime](../concepts/agent-runtime.md), [Dispatch and Submission](../concepts/dispatch-and-submission.md), [RFC 0002](../../rfcs/0002-compiler-architecture/design.md), [RFC 0007](../../rfcs/0007-agent-runtimes-and-execution-backends/design.md), [RFC 0008](../../rfcs/0008-scheduler-and-capacity-policy/design.md), [`policy/scheduler.yaml`](../../policy/scheduler.yaml), [`backends/`](../../backends/README.md).\\n\",\n    \"docs/explanation/no-daemon-runtime.md\": \"# No-Daemon Runtime\\n\\nPurpose: explain why Striatum-next has no daemon.\\n\\n## The ruling\\n\\nStriatum-next has no daemon. The Driver is an invoked program over the graph and ledger, serialized by the Graph Store's crash-released locks. There is no process whose uptime is a truth condition ([RFC 0006](../../rfcs/0006-driver-control-surface/design.md)).\\n\\nThe principle beneath the ruling: **shared truth scales better than shared mutable state.** A daemon exists to guard shared mutable state; Striatum-next shares truth instead — an append-only ledger read without locks, content-addressed bodies copied without coordination, attestations across graphs instead of a shared store. And shared truth does not eliminate mutable state; it corners it: share truth immutably, and give the residual mutable state — the append tail, the product ref — exactly one owner and one lock, kernel-released on death.\\n\\n## Why the daemon's reasons dissolved\\n\\nStriatum-0's daemon existed to guard a live truth store, to answer lanes mid-run, to sweep for recovery, and to serve live status. Two architectural decisions dissolved all of it. The **Derived-State Doctrine** made truth plain files — the artifact graph and the append-only ledger — with everything else a rebuildable fold, so nothing needs a resident guardian and status is a derived store refreshed on read. **Crash-only lanes** made execution sealed — backends receive sealed work and submit, or nothing — so no lane ever has anything to call mid-run, and recovery collapses to the one invoked verb, `reconcile`.\\n\\nWhat the daemon cost is on the record: daemon-unreachable as a standing failure class, version skew between daemon and clients, socket and token friction, boot parks, store split-brain. An invoked driver cannot be \\\"down\\\": the worst failure is a stale derived store, and the cure is a rebuild, not an incident. The Striatum-0 daemon is a recorded rejected alternative; it does not return.\\n\\n## Locks, leases, wakes\\n\\nCorrectness needs serialization; promptness needs triggers; neither needs residency.\\n\\n- The **append lock** (`ledger/LOCK`) serializes every ledger write; the **drive lease** (`drive.lease`) admits at most one drive session per repository graph. Both live in the Graph Store — never the working tree — and both are kernel-released on process death, so the Driver is itself crash-only: a session killed mid-loop leaves a prefix-valid ledger and no cleanup obligation.\\n- **Wakes** are non-authoritative triggers that invoke `striatum drive`: a standing timer (the documented liveness floor), a backend adapter after committing a submission, a repository hook on watched targets, or the Principal typing the verb. A missed wake delays; it can never corrupt or diverge. Each session additionally rewrites a durable timer unit to its computed next horizon, so promptness survives reboots.\\n\\n## What is deliberately not built\\n\\nNo RPC surface, sockets, or capability tokens — the only mutating boundary is one program operating on files owned by one OS user. No resident status server — machine consumers use the same CLI with `--json`. No second ledger reader — the `striatum` binary is the box's sole ledger reader, which contains version skew structurally.\\n\\nCanonical: [RFC 0006](../../rfcs/0006-driver-control-surface/design.md) · [D0006](../../decisions/D0006-driver-control-surface.md); locks and append discipline: [RFC 0009](../../rfcs/0009-provenance-ledger-and-artifact-store/design.md).
